source: Wang et al. (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI), section 3.3 ablation of callable vs in-memory skills
finding: Gap 3 view. ASI separates two things: whether a skill was verified by execution, and whether it is shown as a note or exposed as a callable action. Verification matters most. Verified text in memory (soft reuse) gets almost all of the callable gain.
numbers: WebArena shopping, claude-3.5-sonnet, success rate: unverified text in memory 32.6; verified program in memory 36.4; verified text in memory 39.0; verified program added as callable action 40.1. Whole benchmark: vanilla 32.7, AWM 36.3, ASI 40.4. Skill induction passes verification on 15.6% of turns for ASI versus 31.4% adding a skill for AWM. Programs shown in memory were often called and failed because they were not in the action space.
quote: improves end success rate by 4.2 points
limits: One backbone, one site for the ablation, no repeats or confidence intervals on that table. No random-example control. The 23.5% in the abstract is relative (40.4 vs 32.7), not points.
agent_relevance: Verification is worth about 6 points; the callable format adds about 1 point over verified prose. Our store should verify first and treat callable exposure as a secondary choice.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, sections 4.1, 4.2, 5 (induction method, text vs code, workflow actions)
finding: Gap 3 view. Replacing LLM abstraction with a rule-based step (dedupe action sequences, drop steps that cannot run) gives the same WebArena score. Text and code workflows score alike. Exposing workflows as callable actions is rarely used.
numbers: WebArena gpt-4: rule-based induction 35.6 success, 6.3 steps; LLM induction 35.5, 5.9 steps (BrowserGym baseline 23.5). Mind2Web cross-task gpt-4 step success: rule 43.4, LM 45.1, text format 45.4; task success 2.0 vs 4.8 vs 3.6. Callable workflow actions (AWM_AS) raise step success by 1.3 (46.4 vs 45.1) but agents call a workflow in only 18.5% of tasks.
quote: agents call workflow actions in merely 18.5% of the tasks
limits: Mind2Web task success is 2 to 5% so differences are a few tasks. Text says AWM_AS success equals 3.2 while the table shows 3.6 vs 4.8, so the paper is internally inconsistent there. No compute-matched arm. Web sites repeat templates.
agent_relevance: Most of the 12-point WebArena gain survives with crude, non-LLM abstraction. This suggests the gain is from showing past successful action sequences, not from clever abstraction.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, section 3.2 comparison with Synapse (retrieved concrete examples)
finding: Gap 3 view. Abstract workflows beat retrieved concrete examples on Mind2Web. The authors say concrete examples bias element choice toward the example. This is the only direct 'abstract routine vs retrieved example' comparison in the AWM paper.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task, gpt-3.5-turbo: AWM element accuracy 39.0 vs Synapse 34.0 (+5.0); step success 34.6 vs 30.6 (+4.0); task success 2.8 vs 2.4. gpt-4: AWM step success 45.1 vs MindAct 36.2. Action F1 is lower for AWM (52.8 vs 56.6 MindAct, gpt-3.5).
limits: Synapse is a different system with its own prompt format; the authors added workflows to its pipeline. Task success numbers are tiny. A random-example control is still missing.
agent_relevance: Abstraction may reduce copying of example-specific details. Strip example-specific values when storing a helper.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, Table 1 and section 3.4 ablations (read in full this session)
finding: Gap 2 and 9 view. Without the skill library the agent is almost as fast early and plateaus later. Self-verification is the most important feedback type. GPT-3.5 as the code writer gives 5.7x fewer items than GPT-4, so the library depends on a strong writer.
numbers: Prompting iterations to reach tech level, mean +/- sd over 3 trials: wooden 6+/-2 (Voyager) vs 7+/-2 (no library); stone 11+/-2 vs 9+/-4; iron 21+/-7 vs 29+/-11; diamond reached 1/3 (102 iterations) vs 0/3. Removing self-verification: -73% discovered items; random curriculum -93%; GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4: 5.7x fewer unique items. GPT-4 is about 15x the price of GPT-3.5.
quote: Self-verification is the most important among all the feedback types
limits: Three trials per arm. No reuse counts. The no-library arm is faster on stone and does not differ much on wooden. Minecraft only.
agent_relevance: The library matters late in a long task stream, not early. Budget a strong model for writing helpers and a verification step; do not expect early gains.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: customizing LLMs by creating and retrieving from specialized toolsets, Tables 2-3 and section 4.3
finding: Gap 2 view. A tool library built by GPT-4 and retrieved at test time gives large gains for GPT-3.5 and much smaller gains for GPT-4 on the same VQA tasks. This is a clean two-backbone test of 'gain shrinks as model gets stronger' outside ReGAL (two backbones here, not three).
numbers: Soft accuracy, ViperGPT baseline to CRAFT. GPT-3.5-Turbo: GQA 35.0 to 45.4 (+10.4), OK-VQA 15.4 to 33.4 (+18.0), A-OKVQA 15.6 to 30.8 (+15.2). GPT-4: GQA 51.4 to 55.6 (+4.2), OK-VQA 36.7 to 39.0 (+2.3), A-OKVQA 32.8 to 35.3 (+2.5).
limits: Two backbones only. Toolset was created by GPT-4 from training examples (not by the test model). No compute match. Tools run image models, so some gain is from tool access, not from learning abstractions.
agent_relevance: Same direction as ReGAL. Expect helper-store gain to be largest on weak or mid models; test on at least three sizes.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT ablations (section 4.1-4.2) and retrieval baselines (Table 2)
finding: Gaps 3 and 5 view. Skipping the abstraction step (store raw solutions as tools) keeps most of the gain on two of three datasets, so retrieved worked examples already carry much of the benefit. Retrieval design matters a lot: matching on function name was the most important view, and plain SimCSE or BM25 over the same toolset were much weaker.
numbers: GPT-3.5 soft accuracy GQA / OK-VQA / A-OKVQA: ViperGPT 35.0 / 15.4 / 15.6; CRAFT 45.4 / 33.4 / 30.8; CRAFT without abstraction 37.1 / 31.0 / 28.0; without problem view 42.4 / 32.7 / 29.8; without function-name view 36.4 / 26.8 / 21.7; without docstring view 37.3 / 29.8 / 25.0. Same toolset with SimCSE retrieval: GQA 36.4, OK-VQA 18.4; BM25: GQA 37.9, OK-VQA 13.4. On TabMWP BM25 reached 89.2, above CRAFT's retrieval.
limits: VQA tasks, tool-calls to vision models. Table text was garbled in extraction; the row-to-column mapping was checked against the text claims (6.6 drop for name ablation, +10.4/+18.0/+15.2 gains). The no-abstraction arm still used GPT-4 to write names and docstrings.
agent_relevance: Use name plus description plus problem text for matching, not one embedding. Raw verified solutions are a reasonable first store; abstraction is an add-on.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, Tables 1-4 and section 4.5
finding: Gap 2 view, opposite direction. When the model writes its own memory, the gain needs a strong base model. Smaller siblings gain little or lose. The authors say a weak model cannot produce reliable strategies to store or read them back.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23.3 to 50.0 (DC-Cu), AIME 2025 6.7 to 36.7, GPQA-Diamond 59.6 to 68.7 (DC-RS). GPT-4o Game of 24 10 to 99 (DC-RS), but GPT-4o GPQA 57.1 to 58.1 and MMLU-Pro slightly down. Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2024 10.0 to 36.7 (DC-Cu) but 26.7 of that comes from DC- (instructions, empty memory); AIME 2025 0.0 to 13.3 (DC- already 13.3). GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024 16.7 to 13.3 (DC-Cu and DC-RS below baseline), GPQA 34.3 to 32.3. DeepSeek R1 and o1: minimal or inconsistent gains.
quote: smaller models, such as GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku, generate correct solutions less reliably
limits: AIME 2024 and 2025 have 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points. Very few runs. Retrieval failures were seen when examples were only loosely related. Haiku is better read as 'instructions help, memory adds a little'.
agent_relevance: Memory that the model writes itself needs a competent model. Do not assume a small model benefits. Compare with an empty-memory arm that has the same instructions.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, majority-voting comparison (Table 4) and token footnote 13
finding: Gaps 1 and 10 view. DC beats 3-sample majority vote, but the vote adds nothing here, and the cheatsheet arm spends far more output tokens per query than baseline. Half of the gain is from the structured prompt with empty memory. So the memory-versus-sampling test is not compute matched.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 / 2025: baseline 23.3 / 6.7; majority vote of 3 on baseline 23.33 / 6.7; DC- (instructions, no memory) 36.7 / 23.3; majority vote on DC- 33.3 / 23.3; DC-Cu 50.0 / 36.7. Average output tokens per query on AIME 2024: baseline 370, DC- 494, DC-RS 1035, DC-Cu 1831. Full-history append instead of curated memory: Sonnet 26.7 vs 50.0; GPT-4o 6.7 vs 40.0 (baseline 20.0).
quote: MV ... yielded no improvements over single-shot inference
limits: 30 questions per exam. Token counts are output tokens only as stated. The vote used n=3 (about 3x tokens) while DC-Cu used about 5x tokens, so the arms differ in cost. The paper itself says token savings come later, but gives no break-even point.
agent_relevance: The memory gain over the instructions-only arm is 13.3 points on both exams. At 3x to 5x tokens a larger vote may close part of it. Run the matched-token test ourselves.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, discussion of error clustering and curation
finding: Gap 9 and 6 view. Wrong stored heuristics are reused and amplified when similar tasks come up. Stuffing every past turn into the prompt is worse than curating. The authors name pruning as needed but give no rule.
numbers: Full-history (uncurated) vs curated: Sonnet AIME 2024 26.7 vs 50.0; GPT-4o 6.7 vs 40.0, below its own baseline 20.0. Models sometimes wrote 'Previous content [...] preserved' instead of rewriting memory, which degraded stored notes.
quote: faulty heuristics that slip into memory can be equally amplified
limits: Qualitative remark; no measured rate of harmful reuse.
agent_relevance: Add a curation step that rewrites, not appends. Keep a way to delete a stored item.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory, Tables 1 and 4
finding: Gap 3 view and an independent test of AWM and Dynamic Cheatsheet. In four embodied multi-turn benchmarks, plain retrieval of past experiences as examples (ExpRAG) beat the procedural-abstraction methods, and AWM and DC were no better than a ReAct baseline. This is a different group from the AWM authors.
numbers: Average success / progress over AlfWorld, BabyAI, PDDL, ScienceWorld. Gemini 2.5 Flash: ReAct 0.32/0.56, AWM 0.30/0.53, DC-Cu 0.29/0.53, DC-RS 0.30/0.54, ExpRecent 0.39/0.59, ExpRAG 0.46/0.63, ReMem 0.50/0.64. Claude 3.7 Sonnet: ReAct 0.57/0.79, AWM 0.49/0.74, DC-Cu 0.49/0.75, DC-RS 0.50/0.75, ExpRecent 0.58/0.79, ExpRAG 0.63/0.82, ReMem 0.78/0.91. Claude 3.5 Haiku: ReAct 0.27/0.55, AWM 0.23/0.49, ExpRAG 0.51/0.67, ReMem 0.51/0.69.
quote: ExpRAG serves as a simple yet highly effective baseline, outperforming several more complex designs
limits: ExpRAG and ReMem are the benchmark authors' own methods. Implementations of AWM and DC were re-made by them, so they may be weaker than the originals. Cost reported only as tens of thousands of dollars in total. No token-matched arm.
agent_relevance: Raw-experience retrieval is a strong baseline that any abstraction scheme must beat. Include it as an arm.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory, sections 4.2 (task similarity, steps, failures) and B.2 (pruning)
finding: Gaps 2, 6, 9, 10 view. Gain tracks task similarity. Smaller models benefit most (authors' claim, contradicting Dynamic Cheatsheet). Storing failed experiences unfiltered hurts the baselines. Step counts fall with memory. Pruning rates reported but not tied to accuracy.
numbers: Correlation of ReMem gain with within-dataset task similarity: Pearson 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Steps on AlfWorld 22.6 to 11.5 with ReMem. Pruning rates: GPQA 36.8%, AIME 17.5% and 10.8%. Easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy order: ReMem 0.77/0.92 vs 0.81/0.94 on average success/progress (AlfWorld+ScienceWorld).
limits: Pruning section is descriptive, no ablation of pruning against score. The claim that smaller models benefit most is about the authors' own methods.
agent_relevance: Memory pays off when tasks repeat in structure. Measure task similarity before spending on a store.

source: Ho et al. (2025) ArcMemo: abstract reasoning composition with lifelong LLM memory, Table 1 and Table 4
finding: Gap 4 and 1 view. LLM-written concept memory on ARC-AGI-1 gives a small gain that shrinks as inference compute grows. A simple cheatsheet is as good at high retry counts. Only ArcMemo-PS is above baseline at every compute scale tested, but by margins inside the noise at 1 and 2 retries.
numbers: 100-task subset of ARC-AGI-1 public eval, o4-mini (medium), official oracle@2, mean of 3 runs. No retry: baseline 55.17 (sd 3.18), cheatsheet 57.67, ArcMemo-OE 56.67, ArcMemo-PS 59.33 (+4.2, 7.5% relative). One retry: baseline 66.67, cheatsheet 65.67, OE 65.67, PS 67.33 (+0.7). Two retries: baseline 69.00, cheatsheet 71.33, OE 67.67, PS 70.83 (+1.8; cheatsheet higher than PS). Seeded with 160 human-written solutions from a prior dataset.
quote: The marginal impact of memory is reduced with more inference compute
limits: Row mapping from a garbled table reconstructed from Table 1 totals. Only 100 tasks and sd of 1.5 to 3.8 points. Memory is fixed in most runs. Memory runs use similar or more output tokens than baseline (their Figure 4 text). Strict scoring gives about the same picture.
agent_relevance: On ARC the abstraction store is not proven to beat extra sampling. The evidence for gap 4 is weak positive at low compute, null at high compute.

source: Ho et al. (2025) ArcMemo, selection ablation (Table 2), continual update (Table 3), appendix C on embedding retrieval
finding: Gaps 4, 5 view. Reasoning-based selection of stored concepts helps at low compute and saves tokens; plain embedding retrieval of abstract concepts failed. Updating memory during the test stream helped only at high retry counts. In a manual review, 60% of the cheatsheet's new solves had no matching note in the cheatsheet; 100% of ArcMemo's did.
numbers: Selection ablation oracle@2: no retry 59.33 with selection vs 55.17 without; one retry 67.33 vs 66.00; two retries 70.83 vs 70.00 (differences within sd). Continual update (every 10 problems), ArcMemo-OE oracle@2: no retry 56.67 vs 56.00; one retry 65.67 vs 65.00; two retries 67.67 vs 70.00. Embedding retrieval with o3-mini solver: 0.26 to 0.22 (15% drop), retrieved items mostly irrelevant and a few generic concepts were over-retrieved. Specificity pilot (n=10 tasks): maximum-detail concepts solved 4/10, less detail fewer.
limits: Tiny pilots (n=10). 10 differing puzzles in the cheatsheet comparison, so the 40% / 100% figures rest on 5 puzzles per side.
agent_relevance: Use an LLM step to pick helpers, not cosine similarity over abstract text. Tension: more specific helpers solve more but are harder to retrieve.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2025) ARC Prize 2024 technical report
finding: Gap 4 view. No top ARC Prize 2024 entry used library learning. Gains came from test-time training (53.5% for the winner on the private set) and from LLM sampling of thousands of Python programs (about 42% public). A hand-built DSL (Hodel) improved search. The report asks for compute to be reported with every score.
numbers: Brute-force DSL ensemble of 2020 entries: 49% private; best single such submission 40%. Greenblatt: 42% on the public leaderboard, GPT-4o, thousands of programs per task. MindsAI: 33% to 55.5%. ARChitects 53.5%, Akyurek et al. 47.5%. Estimate: 85% reachable by about 100,000,000 programs per task (multi-million dollars for 100 tasks).
limits: Report, not an experiment. Absence of library methods is not evidence they fail; it shows nobody has made them compete.
agent_relevance: On ARC, raw sampling and test-time training are the baselines to beat at matched compute.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2025) SOAR: self-improving language models for evolutionary program synthesis, a case study on ARC-AGI
finding: Gap 4 view. A competing route to improvement on ARC does not store a library at all. It samples and refines programs, then fine-tunes the model on hindsight-relabelled attempts. It reached 52% of the public test set. It needs weight updates, so it is not usable in our no-training scaffold.
numbers: 52% on ARC-AGI public test set with open models (abstract). I read the abstract and method outline, not every table.
limits: Parameter updates are the learning mechanism. Not a library method. Only abstract-level numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Reminds us that failed attempts can be relabelled as valid problem-solution pairs. A text version of that is cheap to test.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: web agents can self-improve by discovering and honing skills, Tables 1-2 and section 4.2
finding: Gaps 2 and 10 view. Skills written and tested by GPT-4o, handed to GPT-4o-mini, help the weaker agent more in relative terms. Opposite to Dynamic Cheatsheet because here a strong model builds the library. Building costs 160 exploration iterations per website.
numbers: WebArena average success: GPT-4o 22.6 to 29.8 (+32%); GPT-4o-mini 9.2 to 14.1 (about +54%); mini plus skills beats GPT-4o without skills on Map, Shopping, Reddit. Live sites (Online-Mind2Web) 40.2 to 56.2 (+39.8%); Car site 0% change. Synthesized APIs matched human APIs on low and medium API-support sites and fell short on GitLab and Maps. Skills are produced by unit-test honing (Stage III).
limits: The text mislabels relative gains (39.8% is the live-site figure, not WebArena). One run per cell. Pre-explored libraries per site, not a task stream. No compute match with 160 exploration iterations. GPT-4o only as builder.
agent_relevance: A strong-model builder plus weak-model user splits cost sensibly. Verify and test helpers before sharing them.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior, Table 1 and sections 3-4
finding: Gap 9 view. Adding every experience to memory without a quality check lowers performance below a small fixed memory. Agents copy outputs of retrieved items with similar inputs (error propagation). Strict (oracle) filtering gives the best results. Cheap LLM judges can hurt.
numbers: Success (fixed small memory / add-all / strict filter): RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Coarse LLM judges C1/C2/C3: EHRAgent 26.19/32.21/34.66; AgentDriver 36.92/40.01/47.37. A fine-tuned judge on 300 labelled examples did best. Input-output similarity correlation about 1 for the synthetic agent.
quote: LLM agents display an experience-following property
limits: Memory is episodic examples (query and output), not helper functions. 'Strict' means ground-truth comparison, a stand-in for human labels. Four agents of mixed type.
agent_relevance: A verification gate before storing is worth more than store size. A weak LLM judge can be worse than a small seeded memory.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) memory management study, section 4 deletion experiments (Table 2)
finding: Gap 6 view. First measured deletion rule. History-based deletion: delete a record once it has been retrieved at least n times (5 here) and its average downstream utility is below a threshold. Combined with periodic deletion it cuts memory size about 4x with equal or better score when the utility judge is reliable. With a weak LLM judge it can hurt.
numbers: EHRAgent, strict evaluator: no deletion 38.67 at 1012 records; periodic 38.59 at 302; history-based 42.06 at 784; combined 42.34 at 248. AgentDriver strict: no deletion 51.00 at 1178; combined 49.97 at 323. CIC-IoT strict: 85.40 at 904 vs 85.50 at 188 combined. With coarse GPT-4o-mini judge, history-based deletion helped EHRAgent but hurt AgentDriver. Settings: minimum retrieval count 5, utility threshold 0.3 to 0.7 depending on agent, periodic every 200 to 500 steps.
limits: Row labels in the extracted table were interleaved, so only the EHRAgent, AgentDriver and CIC-IoT strict rows above were taken, matching the paper's text. Episodic memory, not helper code.
agent_relevance: Gives a candidate rule: keep an item until it has been used about five times, then drop it if later tasks show it does not help. Needs a trustworthy per-use outcome.

source: Shi et al. (2025) Retrieval models aren't tool-savvy: benchmarking tool retrieval for LLMs (ToolRet), abstract and section 6.1
finding: Gap 5 view. Tool retrieval from large sets is hard. Strong text retrievers do poorly, and lexical BM25 can beat ColBERT. Retrieval errors lower the end-task pass rate. Re-ranking helps little.
numbers: 7.6k retrieval tasks, 43k tools. All tested retrievers under 52% recall@10 and under 35% completeness@10; NV-Embed-v1 (7B) under 45% completeness@10. Pilot on ToolBench: replacing the oracle toolset with retrieved tools lowers GPT-3.5 pass rate by about 10 points (figure 1 label: 10.1 decrease). Training on a 200k-instance set improves retrievers.
limits: Corpus is 43k tools from public APIs, much bigger than an agent's own store of tens of helpers. Text from figure 1 was garbled; the 10.1 figure is read from the figure label.
agent_relevance: For small self-made stores, a descriptive name and docstring may be enough. For large stores expect poor embedding recall. Measure retrieval hit rate directly.

source: Bellur, Alghamdi, Workneh, Izraelevitz (2024) Leroy: library learning for imperative programming languages
finding: Gap 8 view. The only found attempt to run Stitch on Python. Stitch needs a Lisp-like form. After converting Python ASTs, most candidates are invalid and compression is almost nil. Nothing was tried on LLM traces.
numbers: Corpus: 122 small Python programs (average 7 lines) from a compiler class. Pruned 3,123 macro-like abstractions, 32 with invalid parameters, about 42,000 smaller than 20 AST nodes. Compression ratio 1.04x excluding library; corpus grew 1.2% when the library is counted.
limits: Toy corpus, subset of Python, student code, compression only (no downstream solving). Not LLM output.
agent_relevance: No evidence that symbolic compression of an agent's own code or prose traces works. Expect heavy filtering and small gain on short, varied snippets.

source: Lopez-Miguel, Happe, Cito, Bartocci, Koenighofer, Tappler (2026) ATLAS: discovering agent strategies through LLM-guided abstraction and automata learning
finding: Gap 8 and 2 view. LLM categorises raw agent steps into abstract labels, then a Markov chain is learned from 20 runs per machine. Strategy hints from a frontier model's chain, fed step by step to a small model, lift the small model strongly. Large bulky hints hurt the 8B model. Not Stitch, but the closest trace-compression work found.
numbers: 12 vulnerable VMs, 5 tests each (60 runs per mode). ministral-8b success: no hints 5.0%, common path 1.7%, minimal 8.3%, guided 8.3%, dynamic (one step at a time, tracking chain state) 28.3%. ministral-14b: no hints 1.7%, common path 11.7%, minimal 11.7%, guided 21.7%, dynamic 38.3%. Model compression 57 to 7 states, 41 to 7 states in two examples.
limits: Seven-page case study at MODELS 2026, pen-testing only, one benchmark, no repeats, no compute match. Abstraction needs a strong LLM for category discovery.
agent_relevance: Feeding one stored step at a time with state tracking beats dumping a whole strategy on a small model. Candidate design for the helper store with weak executors.

source: Wang et al. (2023/2024) LEGO-Prover, Table 1 and section 4.2 (checked against the replication's citation)
finding: Resolves the open question on the replication's quote. The original paper's own text gives 52.4% valid and 45.5% test with model-written informal proofs, 55.3% and 50.0% with human-written ones, and 57.0% and 50.0% as a cumulative figure. So '45.5% (50% with human proofs)' is a fair citation. The 52.4% in the earlier note is LEGO-Prover's own model-proof valid score, not the Subgoal-Learning row.
numbers: Subgoal-Learning 48.0 valid / 45.5 test (7.3 and 4.5 point gaps to the human-proof result). Library ablation at 50 attempts on valid: 50.4 with library, 47.1 without. Authors estimate about 300 US dollars for one 100-attempt run. Gap between arms is small early and widens as the library grows.
limits: Table layout was garbled in extraction; the mapping is fixed by the paper's own sentences about 7.3% and 4.5% improvement. The ablation removes the evolver along with the library, which later critics call too aggressive.
agent_relevance: Do not read this as a mis-citation. The earlier correction a32 should say: 52.4 is LEGO-Prover (model proofs) valid, not Subgoal-Learning.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Gap 1 baseline. With a checker, simply sampling more raises coverage log-linearly over four orders of magnitude, including on formal proofs. Without a checker, majority voting and reward models plateau after a few hundred samples (voting after about 100). So a fair compute-matched arm must say whether it has a verifier.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples (above single-sample state of the art 43%). Coverage tested on MiniF2F, CodeContests, MATH, GSM8K with up to 10,000 samples per problem.
limits: Coverage is an upper bound set by the verifier; selection without a verifier plateaus. No library comparison in the paper.
agent_relevance: With a verifier available (tests, proof checker), the match-compute baseline is verified resampling, not majority voting. Choose the baseline to match what the helper store can use.
